title: Countable and Uncountable Sets
quickIdea: A set is countable when its elements can be listed in a sequence, which is the same as a bijection with the natural numbers. The integers and the rationals can be listed; the reals cannot.
remember: A set is countable if it is finite or there is a bijection between it and the natural numbers. Countably infinite means infinite and countable.
The integers are countable: list 0, 1, -1, 2, -2, ... so that every integer appears at a finite position.
The rationals are countable: write the positive rationals in a grid of numerator against denominator and walk the diagonals, skipping repeats.
A countable union of countable sets is countable, and a finite product of countable sets is countable. In particular the set of pairs of natural numbers is countable.
Every subset of a countable set is countable; a superset of an uncountable set is uncountable.
The reals are uncountable (Cantor's diagonal argument): any listing of reals can be defeated by changing the diagonal digit.
The power set of the natural numbers is uncountable and has the same cardinality as the reals.
The set of all finite subsets of the natural numbers is countable, but the set of all infinite subsets is uncountable.
Density is not cardinality: the rationals are dense in the reals and still countable, so 'there is one between any two' proves nothing about size.

example.prompt: Is the set of all ordered pairs of natural numbers countable? Is the set of all subsets of the natural numbers countable?
example.work: For pairs, walk the anti-diagonals of the grid: (0,0), then (1,0), (0,1), then (2,0), (1,1), (0,2), and so on. Every pair sits on exactly one diagonal, so the walk lists them all, which gives a bijection with the naturals. For subsets, apply the diagonal argument to the characteristic functions: no listing of all 0/1 sequences can be complete.
example.answer: The pairs are countable; the set of all subsets of the naturals is uncountable.

gateAngle: GATE has tested countability inside Theory of Computation rather than inside sets: questions about the set of all Turing machines, of all C programs, or of all recursively enumerable languages are countability questions in disguise. This card supplies the set-theoretic argument those questions rely on.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Which of these are countable: the integers, the rationals, the reals, the set of all finite strings over {0,1}, the set of all infinite 0/1 sequences?
variations.answer: The integers, the rationals and the finite strings are countable. The reals and the infinite 0/1 sequences are not.
variations.why: Finite strings over a finite alphabet are a countable union of finite sets, one set per length. Infinite 0/1 sequences correspond to subsets of the naturals, which are uncountable.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is an arbitrary union of countable sets always countable?
variations.answer: No. A countable union of countable sets is countable, but an arbitrary union need not be.
variations.why: Each real number is a countable (singleton) set, and the union of these sets over all reals is the set of reals, which is uncountable. The hypothesis 'countably many' is doing real work.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Is the set of all functions from the natural numbers to {0, 1} countable?
variations.why: Such a function is an infinite 0/1 sequence, and the diagonal argument shows that no listing of all sequences can exist. This is the same argument that makes the power set of the naturals uncountable.

trap.what: Assuming a set is uncountable because it is dense or infinite, or assuming that a subset of a countable set might be uncountable.
trap.why: Cardinality is decided by the existence of a listing, not by density or by how many elements sit between two given ones. Subsets cannot be larger than their supersets, so a subset of a countable set is always countable.
trap.counterexample: The rationals are countable although between any two rationals there is another; the interval of reals between 0 and 1 is uncountable although it is a subset of the reals, showing that the direction of the subset relation matters.

check.question: Is the set of all finite subsets of the natural numbers countable?
check.explanation: For each k the k-element subsets form a countable set, and the whole collection is the countable union over k of those sets, which is countable. The infinite subsets, by contrast, are uncountable.

sources.title: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, ch. 2 (basic structures: sets, set operations, functions)
Grimaldi, Discrete and Combinatorial Mathematics, ch. 3 and ch. 5 (sets, relations, functions)
